The juvenile life stage of the silver scabbardfish (Lepidopus caudatus) is characterized by a rapid initial growth that eventually reaches very large dimensions in mature females. Field surveys and capture records indicate that the ultimate total length attained by females can be as great as 210 centimeters [Li = 210 centimeters], a size that places the species among the larger members of its family. This maximum recorded size contrasts markedly with the remarkably small mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, which emerges from a pelagic egg that is roughly one millimeter in diameter and exhibits a wet weight at birth of only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. Such a prodigious disparity between neonatal mass and adult body mass implies an extraordinarily high relative growth rate over the course of the lifespan. At the other end of the size spectrum, the ultimate wet weight for a large female has been documented at up to 8,000 grams [Wwi = up to 8,000 grams], a value that corresponds to the heaviest published records for the species and underscores the considerable morphological variation between early larval stages and fully grown reproductive individuals.

Reproductive maturation in the silver scabbardfish exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in the timing of pubertal development. Estimates derived from gonadal inspection of captured individuals show that females attain the total length at puberty at 111 centimeters [Lp = 111 centimeters], whereas males become mature at a noticeably smaller body size, with the total length at puberty for males documented at 97 centimeters [Lp = 97 centimeters]. This pattern, in which females delay the onset of sexual maturation until they have reached a larger somatic dimension than males, is common among teleosts that exhibit a fecundity advantage to larger body size. Investigations conducted at a stable water temperature of 12.1 °C [T = 12.1 °C] yielded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 4% [GSI = 4%].

The early developmental chronology of the species, particularly the duration of the embryonic and yolk-sac larval stages, is strongly conditioned by ambient temperature. Comparative data drawn from the closely related Trichiurus nanhaiensis suggest that the interval from egg fertilisation to the onset of exogenous feeding occurs over approximately 3.29 days [ab = approximately 3.29 days] at an incubation temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This value represents the period during which the developing embryo relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and first feeding becomes possible. Following the transition to exogenous feeding, the free-swimming larva enters a planktonic phase that persists for several weeks, during which the tiny larva, weighing a mere fraction of a gram, must locate and capture suitable zooplanktonic prey. Mortality during this early pelagic larval phase is presumed to be extraordinarily high, as is typical for marine teleosts that broadcast spawn and produce small, yolk-poor eggs. The short embryonic period at 20 °C likely confers an advantage by minimizing the window of vulnerability for the demersal egg before eclosion.

Lifespan estimates for the silver scabbardfish have been developed from otolith-based age readings and length-frequency analyses conducted on populations inhabiting temperate waters. The maximum recorded longevity for the species, based on growth increment data collected at an ambient temperature of 12.1 °C [T = 12.1 °C], reaches approximately 2,920 days [am = approximately 2,920 days]. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly eight years, is consistent with the life history strategy of a moderately long-lived, iteroparous pelagic predator that invests in multiple spawning events across its reproductive lifespan rather than a single, semelparous episode. The relatively late age at first reproduction, coupled with the substantial ultimate size of females, suggests that individuals allocate considerable resources to somatic growth during the sub-adult years before shifting investment toward gamete production. The longevity of the species may also reflect the relatively stable thermal environment of the deeper continental shelf waters it typically inhabits, where seasonal temperature fluctuations are less extreme than in surface or coastal zones.

At a thermal regime of 12.1 °C [T = 12.1 °C], the gonadosomatic index of 4% [GSI = 4%] has been observed in pre-spawning females. The ultimate wet weight for female silver scabbardfish, which can reach 8,000 grams [Wwi = 8,000 grams], is thus a critical determinant of reproductive output, as larger individuals are capable of producing a greater volume of eggs. In comparing these life history traits to those of the closely related Trichiurus nanhaiensis, the estimated age at birth of 3.29 days [ab = 3.29 days] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] aligns with the rapid developmental rates typical of tropical and warm-temperate trichiurid species. Overall, the species exhibits a life history characterized by extreme size disparity between life stages, a moderate lifespan, and a size-dependent reproductive strategy that prioritizes growth before the onset of maturation.
